1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6.background: First recorded by Giulio Cesare Polerio around 1580. Also known as the Prussian Defence, its theory was developed extensively in the 19th century.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3.strategy: The solid main line: a pawn defends e4 and the c1-bishop's diagonal opens, and White avoids the early tactics of the sharper fourth moves. White builds the centre slowly, aiming for a manoeuvring game and a central break once the pieces are ready.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Modern Bishop's Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3.background: Sometimes called the Modern Bishop's Opening, because it is commonly reached from the Bishop's Opening by 2.Bc4 Nf6 3.d3 Nc6 4.Nf3. It became popular in the 1980s and has been used by John Nunn and others.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4.strategy: Opens the centre at once and offers a pawn for development: if Black takes, White plays for the initiative with open lines towards f7. A sharp, open game in which Black has to keep an eye on the king and cannot afford loose play.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Open Variation

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5.strategy: Piles up on f7 with knight and bishop before the rest of the army is out, forcing Black to sacrifice a pawn or take wild risks. It is the sharpest test of the Two Knights: Black equalises with accurate play, but a player who misses the point loses quickly.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Knight Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5.background: Known since the 17th century: games with it are attributed to Giulio Cesare Polerio and Gioachino Greco. Siegbert Tarrasch called it "bungling".

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move, but it allows the fork trick: Black takes on e4 and, after the recapture, plays ...d5 to hit bishop and knight at once, reaching an easy, level game. Sound but second-rate, since White has handed Black a simple route to equality.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3.name: Four Knights Game: Italian Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3.background: Popular in the 1880s, though some authors regard it as inferior; Nigel Short used it successfully against Antoaneta Stefanova in 2003.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.O-O.strategy: Castles and offers the e4-pawn for an open position and quick development, but the compensation is thin: Black takes the pawn, answers the threats and keeps it. A dubious gambit that is not worth the pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 Bc5.strategy: Puts the bishop on its most active diagonal, aimed at f2, and reaches the quiet position that 3...Bc5 4.d3 Nf6 produces. Both sides build slowly: White prepares a central break and Black's well-placed pieces keep the answer to it ready, a long fight for the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 Be7.strategy: A solid, modest set-up: the bishop stays behind the pawns and gives up the active diagonal against f2. Black is a little passive but safe, in a slow manoeuvring game.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 Be7.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Modern Bishop's Opening

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 h6.strategy: Takes the g5 square from White's bishop and knight, so there is no pin on the f6-knight and no pressure on f7 from g5, and it may prepare a kingside pawn advance later. It costs a tempo in development: playable, but slow.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4.name: Scotch Game: Scotch Gambit, Dubois Réti Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4.strategy: Takes the offered pawn: the e4-pawn is now attacked by the knight and nothing defends it, so White has to push the pawn or sacrifice it for development. Black has the extra pawn and the central tension is gone, but must defend against White's quick play.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 d6.strategy: Defends e5 without releasing the tension, declining the gambit. It keeps Black solid but passive: White can simplify by trading queens into a drawish game, or gain space by pushing the d-pawn at the c6-knight.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 d6.name: Italian Game: Scotch Invitation Declined

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3 Nxe4.strategy: Grabs the pawn with a knight that White can take, and that is the idea: after the recapture ...d5 forks bishop and knight, so Black regains the piece with a good game. The sacrifice is only temporary, and it is why this fourth move is judged inferior.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Knight Attack, Normal Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5.strategy: Blocks the c4-f7 diagonal with a pawn, the soundest way to meet the threat to f7. Black gives up a pawn after exd5 but gets active pieces and time to develop, and with accurate play Black reaches at least equality.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Traxler Counterattack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5.background: Named after the Czech problemist Karel Traxler, who played it against Reinisch in 1890; in the United States and Britain it is also called the Wilkes-Barre Variation, a name Frank Marshall gave it. No grandmaster has adopted it regularly, though Beliavsky and Shirov have played it in top competition.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5.strategy: A venomous trap: Black ignores f7 and attacks f2, so a greedy Nxf7 runs into ...Bxf2+. But the simple bishop capture on f7 wins a pawn, and Black must prove enough activity for it. Objectively dubious, though no clear refutation is known and it has been played even at top level.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Nxe4.strategy: Grabs the pawn and ignores f7, but the bishop sacrifice drags the king out and a central pawn push follows, leaving Black's king in the middle and in trouble. An unsound gambit that works only if White does not know the refutation.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Nxe4.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Ponziani-Steinitz Gambit

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.O-O Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop to its most active square, where it eyes f2 and discourages White's central break, since a pawn on d4 can be taken. Black declines the sharp pawn grab on e4 and keeps a flexible, natural position.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 h6 5.O-.strategy: Finishes the kingside development and keeps every central plan open; with the game still quiet there is no hurry to commit. The king now stands on the wing where Black's h6 pawn may support a later advance, so White has to watch that plan.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 h6 5.O-.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Modern Bishop's Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 h6 5.O-.strategy: Shores up e5 with a pawn and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal, completing a compact set-up in which the h6 pawn already denies White's pieces the g5 square. Black stays flexible and solid, and the game is a slow fight where neither side has an easy break.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Scotch Game: Scotch Gambit, Advance Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..background: Often adopted by Evgeny Sveshnikov, this line has gradually become the main line of the Open Variation.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: The modern way to play the gambit: the pawn gains space and drives the knight away, so White is not forced to give up e4. Black keeps the extra pawn on d4 for now, but has to spend time on the knight while White's pieces come out with tempo.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Italian Game: Scotch Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: The traditional gambit: White castles and lets Black take e4 for development and pressure down the open e-file. Black's best reply, taking the pawn, gives material back for a level game, so this is sound but offers White little more than equality.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Perreux Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: A tricky second attack on f7 while the pawn still stands on d4. It moves a piece twice and leaves e4 undefended, and Black's counter in the centre forces White to give up castling and to defend, so White is the one who has to be careful.

Hits the c4-bishop with a pawn, so White cannot simply regain the pawn on d4 and has to find a good square for the bishop, while the e5-pawn still attacks the knight. The most natural and common answer: Black keeps the extra pawn and fights for the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Scotch Game: Scotch Gambit, Kingside Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: Steps away from the pawn and hits e5 a second time, with the knight on g4 as well as the one on c6, while eyeing f2. The knight is far from home and f7 is left to the king alone, so it is playable but rarely best; White has to defend e5 and then use the tempo.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Italian Game: Scotch Gambit, Double Gambit Accepted
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: The best reply: Black takes the second pawn and the centre pawns White offered are gone. White's compensation is development and the open e-file, but Black gives material back to settle the position and reaches a comfortable, level game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Italian Game: Scotch Gambit, Janowski Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: Builds a pawn wall and opens the c8-bishop instead of grabbing e4, but it leaves the d4-pawn to be won back at once and gives White the freer pieces. Solid but second-rate: Black has not made use of the extra pawn.

Develops the bishop to its most active square, defends the extra pawn on d4 and aims at f2. It invites the sharp e5 that White is hoping for and reaches a heavily analysed attack by transposition, so Black is theoretically fine but has to walk a narrow path.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Italian Game: Scotch Gambit, de Riviere Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: A modest developing move that prepares to castle and leaves the d4-pawn to White's recapture. Black stays solid and safe but passive, and hands White the freer development.

Steps out of the pawn's attack with a pin: the c6-knight, the only piece guarding d4, cannot move without exposing the king, so White threatens to win the pawn back at once with Nxd4. The main line leads to a sharp, balanced fight with active play for both sides.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Italian Game: Scotch Gambit, Max Lange Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: Puts the knight on the central e4 square, where the d5 pawn supports it and the e5 pawn cannot reach it. Black lets White regain the d4 pawn in exchange for a firm centre and active pieces, and the pin on the c6-knight has to be resolved; the position is sharp but balanced.

Pins the undefended knight on e4 to the king, so Black must block the file at once or lose it. White is two pawns down for the moment, but has the lead in development and open lines in return, and the pawns are soon won back.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Italian Game: Scotch Gambit, Nakhmanson Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: A gambit on a gambit: the knight attacks the one on e4 and offers a piece for an attack on the king if Black takes it. But Black can simply exchange knights and, with the better structure after the recapture on c3, gets the more comfortable game.
Blocks the pin with a pawn that also attacks the c4-bishop. White regains the material, but Black gives back the extra pawn for a safe king and a comfortable, level position.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3 Nxe4 5.strategy: The natural recapture and the main line: White wins the pawn back. Black's reply ...d5 forks bishop and knight, but after the exchanges material is level, so White gets a quiet, equal game and Black the easier play.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3 Nxe4 5.name: Four Knights Game: Italian Variation, Noa Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3 Nxe4 5.strategy: Gives the bishop for a pawn to drag the king out, but after Kxf7 and the recapture on e4 the attack runs out of steam. White has lost the bishop pair and the centre to Black, whose king is safe and whose pawns are strong.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3 Nxe4 5.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3 Nxe4 5.strategy: The fork trick: the pawn attacks both the bishop and the knight, so White cannot keep both, but after the exchanges material comes out level. Black has equalised easily.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5 5..name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Traxler Counterattack, Bishop Sacrifice Line
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5 5..strategy: Takes the pawn with check. The knight on g5 guards the bishop, so the king cannot take it back and must move, losing the right to castle. White is a pawn up against a king stuck in the centre, and Black must make quick development and the pressure on f2 count.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5 5..name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Traxler Counterattack, Knight Sacrifice Line
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5 5..background: The Traxler Counterattack was first seen in the game J. Reinisch against Karel Traxler at Hostouň in 1890, which went through this position with 5.Nxf7 Bxf2+ and ended in checkmate for Black.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5 5..strategy: Takes the pawn and forks the queen and rook, the knight guarded by the bishop on c4. The catch is the answering bishop sacrifice on f2, which drags the king into the open; the complications that follow are thought to be roughly balanced, so White gets a sharp game rather than a clear edge.

The usual answer: the knight on g5 guards the bishop, so the king cannot take it and steps to e7, giving up castling for good. Black is a pawn down with an exposed king, and has to rely on active pieces and the pressure on f2.

The point of the whole line: the bishop takes on f2 with check and drags the white king into the open before the fork on the queen and rook can be used. Black gives a piece for a pawn to gain time and attack the king, and the sacrifice is judged to hold the balance.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5 5..name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Traxler Variation, Trencianske-Teplice Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5 5..strategy: Opens the centre at the price of giving back the extra pawn: d4 attacks the bishop on c5 and the e5 pawn while Black's king is stuck on e7. It leaves the bishop on f7 held only by the knight on g5, so White risks more than a simple retreat would.

Accepts the sacrifice and leaves the king on the exposed f2-square, where a knight check follows at once. White is a piece up for the moment but must survive the attack, and the main lines are thought to end level, so this is a risky way to win material.

Takes a second pawn with check and keeps the white king in the open. The knight on f7 still hits the queen and rook, but grabbing the rook on h8 can end in mate, so White has to choose the king's square with care while Black brings the queen into the attack.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: Takes the pawn and ends both threats at once: the d-pawn no longer attacks the bishop or the e4 pawn. White is a pawn up, and Black's compensation is quick development and the initiative rather than material.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Polerio Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.background: 5...Na5 has also been called the Chigorin Gambit.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: The main line: the knight leaves the pawn's attack with a threat against the bishop, and Black gives up the pawn for lead in development and pressure. The knight stands on the edge of the board for now, but White's extra pawn is hard to hold without care.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Fritz Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.background: The German master Alexander Fritz suggested 5...Nd4 to Carl Schlechter, who published analysis of it in the Deutsche Schachzeitung in 1904 and concluded that it was fully viable. P. S. Leonhardt disputed this assessment in 1907.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: Moves the knight out of the pawn's attack to a central square instead of regaining the pawn. White stays a pawn ahead, but the knight can be hit by c3 and has few safe retreats, so Black often has to trade or sacrifice it. A sharp game with little margin for error.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Ulvestad Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.background: The American master Olav Ulvestad introduced 5...b5 in a 1941 article in Chess Review.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: Offers a second pawn to pull the bishop away from d5 and f7. If White takes it, Black wins the d5 pawn back with an attack on the bishop and the g2 pawn. White's precise answer retreats the bishop to f1, and Black is left to prove the compensation.

Regains the pawn at once, but the knight on d5 only blocks the bishop's diagonal for the moment and leaves f7 weak. White can choose between a violent knight sacrifice on f7 and a calm central pawn strike, both hard to meet over the board, so the move is too risky.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Kloss Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: Adds a second attacker on d5, but Black is already a pawn down and the knight on b4 is easily chased away, so there is no clear compensation. White simply plays on with the extra pawn while Black has to hope for tactics.

Counter-intuitive, but the only good answer: the bishop leaves the attacked square and guards g2, so a queen capture on d5 only loses time to a knight development that hits it. White keeps the extra pawn and the pressure on f7 while Black has to prove the compensation.
Chases the knight, but the sacrifice on f7 refutes it: after the king takes, the d-pawn captures the knight on c6, leaving White two pawns up against an exposed king.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Polerio Defence, Bishop Check Line
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: Moves the bishop out of the knight's attack with check, so no time is lost and the extra pawn stays. Black has to block, and the knight on a5 remains on the edge of the board for now, so White keeps a small edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Polerio Defence, Kieseritzky Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.background: Paul Morphy preferred this line, which has been named after Lionel Kieseritzky and is also known as the Morphy Variation.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: Guards the bishop with a pawn to keep the extra pawn instead of retreating. The cost is that the knight can still trade itself for the bishop, doubling White's c-pawns and giving Black the bishop pair, and Black gets active play for the pawn.

The standard block: the pawn attacks the bishop and offers a second pawn. Black gives up material for open lines, a broad centre and active pieces, and plays for long-term pressure while White tries to consolidate the extra pawn.
Questions the knight that has only just come to g5: it must go back, undoing the time White spent attacking f7, and Black gains a tempo. Black gets good chances for the pawn.

Hits the knight with a pawn at once: its retreat squares are poor, so Black must trade it or sacrifice it. White keeps the extra pawn and the pressure on f7, while Black needs active play to justify the pawn.

Answers the attack on the knight with an attack on the bishop: if White simply takes the knight, Black takes the bishop, a trade that removes a key attacker of f7. White keeps the extra pawn but must now retreat the bishop.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Lolli Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.background: Bobby Fischer thought the Lolli Attack, 6.d4, very strong.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: Takes the centre and attacks e5 while keeping the pressure on f7: the knight on d5 is the only piece standing between the bishop and f7. White gets a lasting edge without the complications of a sacrifice.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Fried Liver Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.background: Also called the Fegatello Attack, after an Italian dish. It has been known for many centuries, the earliest known example being a game played by Giulio Cesare Polerio before 1606.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: The knight sacrifices itself to drag the king into the open: it forks the queen and rook, and after the king takes it, a queen check chases the king to the middle of the board. White gets a fierce attack, and defending is much harder than attacking.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Pincus Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.e.strategy: Checks first, so that after the usual block the bishop can return to e7 with an attack on the knight on g5. Black develops with tempo, but White's centre and the weakness on f7 still give White the more comfortable game.

Forced, since the knight on f7 forks the queen and rook. Black wins a piece for a pawn, but the king is dragged to the centre, and the queen check that follows decides whether Black can survive the attack.
